query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A selective thermal treatment—applied just below the bulk phase coarsening temperature—can induce the formation of a thin, ductile interfacial complexion at the lamellar colony boundaries in eutectic high-entropy alloys, thereby reducing stress concentration sites and mitigating microcrack initiation. This modification should improve both the room-temperature tensile strength and ductility relative to the conventional, unmodified lamellar microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase (e.g., FCC/B2) lamellar microstructure produced by conventional processing featuring numerous internal boundaries where microcracks typically nucleate during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: A carefully controlled annealing treatment applied at a temperature just below the threshold for bulk phase coarsening to selectively modify the interfacial regions between lamellar colonies.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation experiments performed on specimens that have undergone the selective thermal treatment versus control specimens with conventional processing.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, coherent, and ductile interfacial complexion that forms along the lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The induced interfacial complexion reduces local stress concentration at the colony boundaries, thereby mitigating microcrack nucleation without altering the high-strength bulk lamellae. This engineering at the interfaces is expected to enable a simultaneous improvement in strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Specimens undergoing the selective thermal treatment will display a higher room-temperature tensile ductility along with maintained or enhanced tensile strength relative to the unmodified baseline, as measured by improvements in tensile strain and stress–strain behavior.
generation.baseline: The conventional eutectic lamellar-colony microstructure produced by standard processing, which exhibits high strength at the expense of ductility due to microcrack initiation at its unmodified internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: The annealing conditions must be precisely controlled (temperature and duration) to prevent bulk phase coarsening or unwanted transformations; the intervention is expected to be effective only if the thermal treatment is limited to modifying the interfaces without altering the overall lamellar structure.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain whether the induced interfacial complexion will be sufficiently stable during extended room-temperature tensile deformation and whether the magnitude of strength and ductility improvement will be large enough to overcome intrinsic brittleness. Additionally, the sensitivity of the outcome to the precise thermal treatment parameters requires further exploration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy specimens: one set processed conventionally and a second set subjected to the selective thermal treatment at a temperature just below the bulk coarsening threshold. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify the formation of a continuous, modified interfacial complexion along the lamellar colony boundaries in the treated specimens. Subsequently, perform room-temperature tensile tests on both sets.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (TEM, APT) to confirm the presence and continuity of the interfacial complexion.
Room-temperature tensile strength, yield strength, and ductility (elongation to fracture).
Stress–strain curve analysis to evaluate the reduction in signs of localized strain or microcrack initiation near the interfaces.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermal treatment fails to produce a continuous, ductile interfacial complexion (as evidenced by microstructural analysis) or if the treated specimens do not show statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the conventional baseline, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Dual-phase high-entropy alloys with excellent room temperature and high-temperature properties have been widely studied as potential high-temperature structural materials. However, interface weakening causes its high-temperature performance to decline at higher temperatures, severely limiting further development. In this study, a series of Al17Cr10Fe36Ni36Mo1Hfx (x = 0, 0.03, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.8 at%) alloys were prepared to study the effect of Hf content on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the matrix alloy. The results indicate that with the addition of the Hf, the Hf-rich phase began to precipitate at the interface and inside the B2 phase in the matrix alloy. In contrast, the morphology of both the FCC and B2 phases had no noticeable change. With the increase in Hf content, the high-temperature strength and ductility of the alloy first increased and then decreased, while the room temperature performance remained almost unchanged. decision.trend: Early work on eutectic high‐entropy alloys established the promise of a fine lamellar, dual‐phase microstructure (e.g., FCC/B2 in AlCoCrFeNi2.1) for attaining high strength with good ductility. Subsequent studies introduced thermo‐mechanical treatments—such as cryo‐rolling with annealing, hybrid (cryo/warm) rolling, and friction stir processing—to further refine grain sizes, modify phase fractions, and promote beneficial deformation mechanisms (e.g., transformation-induced plasticity, microcrack-arresting effects). While these strategies improved the overall balance of strength and ductility, they consistently revealed that the numerous internal lamellar boundaries remain preferential sites for microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
decision.unsolved: The unsolved challenge lies in the intrinsic brittleness at the numerous colony interfaces: despite processing advances that refine microstructure and balance phase fractions, the internal boundaries continue to concentrate stress and nucleate microcracks, thereby limiting tensile ductility even as strength improves.
decision.lever: selective thermal treatment to induce interfacial complexion formation at lamellar colony boundaries
decision.why: Building on the trend where processing methods tailored the bulk lamellar microstructure but did not directly address the weakness at the interfaces, the proposed intervention seeks to thermally engineer the interfacial regions. By applying a targeted annealing protocol (with carefully controlled temperature and duration) just below the threshold for bulk phase coarsening, it is possible to induce the formation of a thin, ductile, and coherent interfacial complexion along the colony boundaries. This modified boundary phase would reduce local stress concentrations—mitigating microcrack nucleation—while preserving the high strength provided by the unaltered lamellae. Prior evidence from studies on dual-phase and heterogeneous alloys suggests that interfacial engineering can relieve stress concentrations and enhance ductility, thereby making this the most plausible next step to simultaneously improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline. An experiment that fails to observe improved ductility (or shows significant coarsening of the phases) under these controlled annealing conditions would falsify the hypothesis.

families.principle: Direct modifications at the internal boundaries—in particular, adjusting interfacial chemistry or structure—can enhance cohesion, reduce stress concentrations, and block the nucleation and propagation of microcracks.

families.best_lever: Engineer the interfaces by applying nanoscale interfacial treatments (e.g., deposition of a ductile interlayer or targeted dopant addition) that enhance boundary bonding, thereby simultaneously boosting strength and tensile ductility.

families.best_lever: Develop a modified casting or additive manufacturing process that controls cooling rates to yield a finer, more uniformly distributed boundary network.

families.principle: Altering the elemental makeup tailors phase stability and enables mechanisms like solid-solution and precipitation strengthening while aiming to concurrently permit ductile deformation. This can also promote beneficial segregation to internal boundaries.

families.best_lever: Introduce a minor alloying addition designed to segregate to internal boundaries and enhance interphase cohesion, reducing stress concentrations.

families.principle: Tailored heat treatments or combined thermal–mechanical protocols can adjust phase distributions and relieve interfacial stresses, potentially ameliorating brittle failure without sacrificing strength.
cues_for: processing considerations and internal boundary stresses could be mitigated by proper thermal regimes
cues_against: conventional thermal and thermomechanical treatments are already part of the baseline, and previous methods have not overcome the trade–off
families.best_lever: Implement a novel annealing protocol (or a sequence with controlled deformation) that selectively relieves boundary stresses while maintaining lamellar integrity.

families.principle: Engineering the spatial layout, colony size, or interlamellar spacing can modulate the stress distribution and crack propagation paths, potentially balancing strength and ductility.
cues_for: the problem is tied to the inherent dual–phase lamellar architecture with numerous internal boundaries
cues_against: the unmodified lamellar-colony architecture is the baseline, and previous microstructural-design strategies have failed to fully overcome the brittle response
families.best_lever: Introduce a controlled gradient or refinement of lamellar spacing to promote a more favorable distribution of strain and delay microcrack initiation.
